At 1e-5 to 1.3e-4 the network is undertrained in 243 epochs, so a larger step size substantially improves accuracy.
Tiny batches give noisy gradients and many updates per epoch, so a larger learning rate becomes unstable.
With a tiny learning rate the model needs many update steps, and a larger batch cuts the number of steps per epoch.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise, which stabilizes training at high learning rates.
Pushing L2 to 0.129 or 1 over-regularizes and underfits, whereas small alpha changes are nearly neutral.
Deeper ReLU networks are more prone to divergence or dead units at large learning rates.
Wider layers amplify effective update size at large learning rates, increasing instability.
Going from 16 to 40 units relieves a capacity bottleneck, while gains from widening saturate at larger widths.
Increasing alpha from tiny values is roughly neutral or slightly helpful, unlike increases at larger alpha that hurt.
